title: Four thoughts that turn the mind
hook: precious human life, death, karma, the faults of samsara

segments.voice: Yesterday: lungta, the wind horse, and wheels and flags that carry the mantra outward. Your line: the wind carries it. Today, the end of the week.

A doctor's call. A birthday with a zero on the end. A friend who was fine last month, and isn't. Most people change direction only after a jolt like that. For a week or two, everything looks different: what matters, what doesn't, how you want to spend your hours. Then the feeling fades and the old grooves take over. Tibetan teachers noticed this long ago, and built the jolt into the very start of the path, on purpose, so it wouldn't depend on bad news.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S CALL. A BIRTHDAY.` → `EVERYTHING LOOKS DIFFERENT.` → `THEN THE OLD GROOVES RETURN.`

segments.voice: In Tibetan practice, four reflections come before everything else, and people return to them for a lifetime. First, precious human life. Tibetan teachers borrow an image the Buddha gives in the Pali discourses: a blind turtle in the great ocean rises to the surface once every hundred years, and a wooden yoke with one hole drifts on the waves. The turtle will put its head through that hole, the Buddha says, sooner than a being who has fallen into the lower realms will win back a human birth. So this life, with the time and freedom to learn anything at all, is rare. Second, death and impermanence. Death is certain; its time is not. Third, karma: actions have results, and the small ones add up. Fourth, the faults of samsara, the round of birth and death: even the good parts don't last, and chasing them never quite satisfies. The twelfth-century teacher Gampopa taught all four in a famous book, and the preliminary practices set them in this order, which matters. First you see how lucky you are. Then how short the time is. Then how much your actions count. Then that more chasing won't fix it. Together, they swing the mind around, like a boat in the current, toward the path. Now look back at the week. For a while. The question is still open. Virtue, calm, wisdom. The elders' day. Then the climb: the diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. And today: turn the mind.
screen: `PRECIOUS HUMAN LIFE.` · `DEATH IS CERTAIN, ITS TIME IS NOT.` · `ACTIONS HAVE RESULTS.` · `CHASING NEVER QUITE SATISFIES.` · then, large: `TURN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the four and stay with it: for precious human life, picture the turtle and the yoke, then look at your own hands, here, with time to sit; for death, rest in the thought that this breath is one of a limited number. Don't push toward a feeling; let the thought sit beside you the way you'd sit beside a friend. When the mind wanders, return to the one you chose.
Gampopa. The twelfth-century teacher who taught the four thoughts in a famous book: precious human life, death, karma, and the faults of samsara.
Your line: turn the mind. Four thoughts, and the boat swings toward the path. That's the week.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite and reflect on the four thoughts at the start of each practice session, and they form the first part of the preliminary practices (ngöndro) taught in all the Tibetan schools.

fork.setup: you've just heard that human life is precious and death's timing unknown. a Tibetan teacher asks what you'll do with that. which answer fits the four thoughts?
options: panic and try to do everything at once.
let it turn the mind toward what matters, steadily.
fork.reveal: the four thoughts aren't meant to frighten but to turn the mind, like a boat in the current, toward the path.

original.note: Tibetan blo ldog rnam bzhi: blo (mind) + ldog (turn back) + rnam bzhi (the four): the four thoughts that turn the mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: gloomy thoughts to make you feel bad.
what it means: four reflections that turn the mind toward the path: luck, urgency, care, and seeing through the chase.

what a scholar hears: Gampopa's Jewel Ornament of Liberation teaches all four early on, after buddha-nature; as the 'common' preliminaries of ngöndro they are shared by Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug alike.
recall: going forth from home into the robes

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 129, Balapandita Sutta (the blind turtle and the yoke)
Gampopa, Jewel Ornament of Liberation (the four thoughts)

notes: The turtle simile also appears at SN 56.47–48; paraphrased. In the Pali version the Buddha compares it to a fool regaining a human birth after falling to lower realms; the simplified framing here should be checked.
The four thoughts are presented in different orders in some texts (e.g. the Kagyu formulation); confirm the order used.
Gampopa (1079–1153) and the Jewel Ornament's structure: confirm.
